publication_scope.blurb: Louis Le Blanc de Beaulieu - Sedan Theological Theses, newly rendered from the 1675 London Latin. Covers De Theologia through Angelorum & Hominum Sanctorum Cultu Romana I-LXXVII and Pars Secunda (Reformata) I-CI, De Primi Hominis Immortalitate I-XXXV, De Justitia Primi Hominis I-LIX, De Libero Hominis Arbitrio in genere I-XLVIII, De Libero Hominis Arbitrio absolute & in se spectato (Scholae Romanae doctrina I-XLIX; Pars Tertia I-XLIII), the theses on reconciling divine concurrence with human freedom I-LIX, on human freedom and divine foreknowledge I-XLIV, and on human freedom and the divine decrees, Part One (middle knowledge) I-LXV, Part Two (the Roman doctors) I-XXXVI and Part Three (the Reformed) I-LI, and on how fallen man's free choice stands toward saving good (I-LX), and on the necessity of grace for moral good in fallen man (Pars Prior I-LIII; Pars Posterior, the Protestant doctrine, I-LIX), and on the various distinctions and senses of grace in the Roman School (I-LXX) and in the Reformed Schools (I-XLIX), and on the Roman School's division of grace into sufficient and efficacious (I-CXLV, complete), and on the Protestant doctrine of that distinction, beginning with the Lutherans of the Augsburg Confession (I-XX). Not the collected folio.
publication_scope.era_note: Le Blanc wrote in the mid-seventeenth century as Reformed professor at the Academy of Sedan. This is not a patristic work. It is a public-domain Latin Reformed retrieval on the same Fathers-site pipeline. The 1675 Pitt folio is Public Domain Mark 1.0. Do not treat the site as ante-Nicene only.

source_text: THESIS I. ILLI Confessionis Augustanae Theologi qui Lutherani appellantur, non admittunt vulgatam gratiae divisionem in sufficientem atque efficacem. Idque quoniam una eademque Dei gratia est quae in credentibus operatur, & ab incredulis repellitur. Adeoque, juxta ipsos, illa ipsa gratia quam aspernantur & conculcant increduli & impoenitentes, ex se & in se efficax est, nec debet tantum sufficiens dici opposite ad quandam gratiam efficacem.
english: Thesis I. The theologians of the Augsburg Confession known as Lutherans reject the familiar division of grace into sufficient and efficacious. Their reason is that the grace of God at work in believers is one and the same as the grace that unbelievers drive away.

On their view, therefore, the very grace that the unbelieving and impenitent scorn and tread underfoot is efficacious of itself and in itself. It should not be called merely sufficient, as if set against some other grace that is efficacious.

source_text: II. Quippe docent Deum omnes quibus verbum praedicatur, quantum in ipso est, velle convertere, & eandem omnibus & singulis offerre gratiam: Verum divinae gratiae & spiritui sancto conversionis opus aggredienti multos resistere: ac propterea gratiam effectum suum in illis non sortiri: alios vero divinam gratiam admittere, & non ponere ipsi impedimentum; unde fit ut gratia sit in ipsis efficax, & conversionem actu in illis efficiat. Sed quoniam ex parte Dei eadem gratia est quae Simonem Petrum convertit, & Simonem Magum non convertit, quoniam alter ipsi restitit, alter non restitit, idcirco unam ab alia non putant esse distinguendam.
english: Thesis II. They teach that God, so far as it rests with him, wants to convert everyone to whom the word is preached, and offers the same grace to all and to each. Many, however, resist divine grace and the Holy Spirit as he sets about the work of conversion, so in them grace does not achieve its effect. Others let divine grace in and put no obstacle in its way, and in them grace is efficacious and actually brings about conversion.

Since, on God's side, the grace that converted Simon Peter is the same grace that failed to convert Simon Magus, the difference being only that one resisted and the other did not, they see no reason to distinguish one grace from the other.

source_text: III. Istud videre est apud Joannem Gerardum Theologum Jenensem tomo secundo tractatu de libero arbitrio capite sexto sectione prima. Concedimus, inquit, sane spiritui sancto conversionis opus aggredienti multos resistere, consilium Dei adversus seipsos spernere, & seipsos vita aeterna indignos judicare, atque hac ratione sua culpa gratiam conversionis a se repellere: sed propterea ipsam gratiam in sufficientem & efficacem dividendam esse negamus, siquidem una eademque Dei gratia est, quae in credentibus operatur, & quae ab incredulis repellitur.
english: Thesis III. This can be found in Johann Gerhard, theologian of Jena, in his second tome, in the treatise on free choice, chapter 6, section 1. 'We readily grant,' he writes, 'that many resist the Holy Spirit as he undertakes the work of conversion, reject God's counsel against themselves, and judge themselves unworthy of eternal life, so that by their own fault they drive the grace of conversion away from themselves.

Yet we deny that grace itself must for that reason be split into sufficient and efficacious, because the grace of God that works in believers and the grace that unbelievers drive away are one and the same.'

source_text: IV. Caeterum ut explicet unde sumatur gratiae Divinae efficacia, observat primo duo extrema cavenda esse; neque enim efficaciam gratiae ad conversionem, tribuendam esse cooperationi voluntatis humanae; nec etiam tribuendam absoluto Dei certos quosdam homines eligentis decreto, sed incedendum via media: quod multi convertuntur & salvantur ad solam gratiam divinam referri debere, quod multi non convertuntur & pereunt, agnoscendum esse ipsorum pereuntium culpa unice fieri: atque in hac pia simplicitate mentem Christianam secure acquiescere posse, etsi ex omnibus difficultatibus non valeret sese expedire.
english: Thesis IV. To explain where the efficacy of divine grace comes from, he first notes two extremes to be avoided. The efficacy of grace for conversion must not be credited to the cooperation of the human will, nor to an absolute decree of God choosing certain particular people. One must take a middle way instead.

That many are converted and saved is to be put down to divine grace alone; that many are not converted and are lost must be recognized as happening only through the fault of those who are lost. In this devout simplicity, he says, a Christian mind can rest secure, even if it cannot find its way out of every difficulty.

source_text: V. Postea vero ostendere conatur quomodo ista inter se constent, efficaciam gratiae divinae non esse tribuendam cooperationi voluntatis humanae, & tamen ejusdem gratiae efficaciam tribuendam quoque non esse Physicae cuidam Dei actioni, qua determinet voluntatem ad volendum & eligendum bonum, quod illi fuit per gratiam excitantem inspiratum. Sic autem ea de re sententiam suam exponit. In conversionis opere Spiritus Sanctus, inquit, tale invenit subjectum, quod nullas habet ad cooperandum vires, siquidem mens hominis nondum renati est caeca, voluntas aversa ac Deo inimica: hoc igitur omni genere medendi atque auxiliandi gratia agit, ut eum quem convertere vult, ex nolente volentem, ex inimico obedientem faciat: illud vero non fit eo modo, ac si homine nec cogitante, nec cognoscente, vel etiam invito hominem convertat, ipsique vim afferat; sed Spiritus Sanctus donat novas vires, quibus assentiri vocationi possit; nec tamen uno statim momento homini adimit veterem illam libertatem, vel potius miseram servitutem, qua oblatam gratiam repudiare possit. Absit igitur ut dicamus, Spiritus Sancti gratiam in conversione Physica quadam actione determinare voluntatem ad volendum & eligendum bonum. Siquidem patitur Spiritus Sanctus sibi resisti, permittit opus suum impediri, videt multos seipsos conversione, & conversionis fructu, ipsa scilicet vita aeterna indignos judicare. Voluntas igitur in omnibus hominibus est post lapsum: ut autem voluntas velit bonum spirituale, id non habet ex suis viribus, siquidem peccato servit: renovat igitur Spiritus Sanctus in conversione hominis voluntatem, ac donat ei novas vires, quibus instructa bonum actu velle & eligere possit: interim ex adhaerente naturae pravitate potest homo nolle bonum, potest Spiritus Sancti opus impedire: ac proinde neutiquam dicendum, quod in conversione Physica quadam actione gratia determinet voluntatem ad volendum ac eligendum bonum. Quippe hac ratione, ut ait idem Doctor, converterentur omnes immutabili necessitate, quos Spiritus Sanctus converti vult. Quod absurdum ille judicat.
english: Thesis V. He then tries to show how two claims fit together: that the efficacy of divine grace is not to be credited to the cooperation of the human will, and yet that it is not to be credited either to some physical action of God that determines the will to will and choose the good which stirring grace has inspired in it. He sets out his view as follows.

'In the work of conversion,' he says, 'the Holy Spirit finds a subject with no strength to cooperate, for the mind of one not yet reborn is blind and the will turned away from God and hostile to him. So the Spirit acts with every kind of healing and helping grace, to turn the one he wants to convert from unwilling to willing, from enemy to obedient. This does not happen as though he converted someone who neither thinks nor knows, or even someone unwilling, by forcing him. Rather, the Holy Spirit gives new strength by which the person can assent to the call, yet does not in one instant take away that old liberty, or better, that wretched slavery, by which he can refuse the grace offered.

We must not say, then, that the grace of the Holy Spirit in conversion determines the will by some physical action to will and choose the good. The Holy Spirit allows himself to be resisted, lets his work be hindered, and sees many judge themselves unworthy of conversion and of its fruit, eternal life itself.

After the fall every person has a will, but the will does not have from its own strength the power to will spiritual good, for it is enslaved to sin. In conversion, then, the Holy Spirit renews a person's will and gives it new strength, so equipped that it can actually will and choose the good. Even so, because of the depravity of nature that still clings to him, a person can refuse the good and can obstruct the Spirit's work. So it must not be said that in conversion grace determines the will by some physical action to will and choose the good.' Otherwise, as the same doctor says, all whom the Holy Spirit wants converted would be converted by unchangeable necessity, which he holds to be absurd.

source_text: VI. Eandem doctrinam tradit & distinctius explicat Georgius Calixtus, antehac Theologiae in Academia Julia Professor, Epitome Theologiae ex ore dictantis excepta. Ibi enim tractatu de ministerio verbi pagina 241. docet, quando minister verbi legalem & Evangelicam doctrinam hominibus proponit, Deum per hoc suum medium & instrumentum efficacem esse, & in cordibus humanis contritionem de commissis peccatis, fiduciam in meritum Christi, peccatorum odium, novaeque vitae studium excitare, nisi tamen ipsi homines suapte pertinacia & pervicacia tenebras magis diligant quam lucem.
english: Thesis VI. Georg Calixtus, formerly professor of theology at the Academia Julia, teaches the same doctrine and explains it more clearly in his Epitome of Theology, taken down as he dictated it. In the treatise on the ministry of the word, page 241, he teaches that when a minister of the word puts the teaching of the Law and of the Gospel before people, God is at work through this means and instrument of his.

Through it God rouses in human hearts sorrow for sins committed, trust in Christ's merit, hatred of sin, and eagerness for a new life, unless people, through their own stubbornness and obstinacy, love darkness more than light.

source_text: VII. Ex ejus enim sententia, nullum dubium est, quin homo oblatam gratiam spernere, rejicere, & Spiritui Sancto fidem operaturo resistere possit. Quoniam Deus homines absoluta sua potentia non trahit & convertit, verum hoc facit secundum ordinem & modum quem semel instituit. Contra vero certum est, hominem posse solicitum esse de sua salute, posse curam suscipere de mediis ad eam, juxta illud, Multi quaerent intrare & non poterunt. Quippe posse hominem audire verbum Dei, imo cum omni alacritate verbum suscipere & scrutari studio discendae & cognoscendae veritatis.
english: Thesis VII. On his view there is no doubt that a person can scorn and reject the grace offered and resist the Holy Spirit when he is about to produce faith, since God does not draw and convert people by his absolute power but according to the order and pattern he laid down once for all.

On the other hand, he holds, it is certain that a person can be anxious for his salvation and can take trouble over the means to it, as in the saying, 'Many will seek to enter and will not be able.' A person can hear God's word, and even receive it with all readiness and study it in an effort to learn and come to know the truth.

source_text: VIII. Hoc autem qui faciunt, eos Deus, secundum hujus Doctoris mentem, majoribus auxiliis dignatur, ut intelligant verbum, ex eo peccata sua agnoscant, & promissionibus Evangelicis fidem habeant: non quidem quod ista qualiscunque opera tantae sit dignitatis aut meriti, sed quod suo verbo Deus eum velit honorem haberi, hunc ordinem servari, & hoc ab homine praestari, priusquam ipse majora & specialiora, & suo genere supernaturalia suppeditet auxilia.
english: Thesis VIII. In this doctor's view, God judges those who do this worthy of greater aids, so that they understand the word, recognize their sins from it, and put faith in the promises of the Gospel.

This is not because such effort, whatever its worth, has any great dignity or merit. It is because God wants his word honoured in this way, wants this order kept, and wants the person to do this much before God himself provides greater and more particular aids, supernatural in kind.

source_text: IX. Distinguit enim author ille inter actiones suo genere supernaturales, id est, quae natura sua vires humanas superant, nec in hominum manu positae sunt, & propterea spiritui sancto sunt ascribendae, quales sunt credere, Deum timere atque diligere, aliaeque similes, quibus constat vera ad Deum conversio: & inter actus quosdam in hominis potestate sitos, quos ab ipso Deus praestari velit, priusquam ad auxilia & dona supernaturalia progressus fiat, saltem quoad modum ordinarium. Quales actus sunt verbum Dei audire, illud scrutari, ad illud attendere, & de mediis ad salutem curam aliquam suscipere.
english: Thesis IX. That author draws a distinction. On one side are actions supernatural in kind: they exceed human strength by their nature, are not in human hands, and so must be credited to the Holy Spirit. Believing, fearing and loving God, and the like, in which true conversion to God consists, are of this sort.

On the other side are certain acts within a person's power, which God wants him to perform before any advance is made to supernatural aids and gifts, at least in the ordinary course. Such acts are hearing God's word, studying it, paying attention to it, and taking some care about the means of salvation.

source_text: X. Credere, inquit, actio est suo genere supernaturalis, sive sua natura supra vires humanas, propterea Spiritui Sancto eam ascribimus, quod is animum humanum ad credendum excitet, efficiatque ut homo credat, diligat, Deum timeat, imo ut credere, timere & diligere velit, atque sic actus supernaturales, veramque conversionem ingredientes, sive constituentes Deo tribuimus, & in manu hominum positos negamus: ita tamen ut non negemus esse quosdam in hominis potestate sitos, quos ab ipso Deus praestari velit, priusquam ad auxilia & dona supernaturalia progressus fiat, certe quoad modum ordinarium.
english: Thesis X. 'Believing,' he writes, 'is an action supernatural in kind, that is, beyond human strength by its nature. We credit it to the Holy Spirit because he rouses the human mind to believe and brings it about that a person believes, loves and fears God, and indeed wants to believe, fear and love.

So we assign to God the supernatural acts that enter into, or make up, true conversion, and we deny that they lie in human hands. We do not deny, however, that some acts lie within a person's power, which God wants him to perform before any advance is made to supernatural aids and gifts, at any rate in the ordinary course.'

source_text: XI. Quibus consona sunt ea quae alibi tradit idem autor. Id autem observandum est, inquit, posito quod Deus Evangelium revelaverit, & passim inter homines praedicari faciat per homines, non esse supra vires naturae quod quis Evangelium audiat, concipiat, consideret, & cum iis quae ab aliis, Judaeis puta vel Mahumetanis, tanquam divinitus revelata proferuntur comparet. In judicio de controversiis Theologicis quae inter Lutheranos & Reformatos agitantur, num. 33.
english: Thesis XI. What the same author teaches elsewhere agrees with this. 'Note,' he writes, 'that once God has revealed the Gospel and has it preached by people far and wide among people, it is not beyond the strength of nature for someone to hear the Gospel, grasp it, think it over, and set it beside what others, Jews for instance or Muslims, put forward as revealed by God.'
This is in his judgment on the theological controversies in dispute between the Lutherans and the Reformed, number 33.

source_text: XII. Itaque juxta ipsum, quicunque verbum audiunt, neque aspernantur consilium Dei in semetipsos, ac verbum Dei non suffocant curis aut divitiis, aut voluptatibus hujus vitae, ii, inquam, Dei opem & operam sentiunt, ejusque gratuita benevolentia ad fidem & vitam deducuntur. Qui vero contra faciunt, suae negligentiae & contumaciae imputare debent, quod a Deo fide non donentur.
english: Thesis XII. According to him, then, all who hear the word, do not reject God's counsel against themselves, and do not smother God's word with the worries, riches or pleasures of this life experience God's help and working, and are brought to faith and life by his free goodwill.
Those who act otherwise must lay it to their own carelessness and defiance that God does not give them faith.

source_text: XIII. Quanquam autem Dei verbum sit instrumentum quo Deus uti solet in hominum conversione, non tamen vult illos ipsos quibus verbum praedicatum non est, omnibus ad salutem mediis destitui: sed Deum sic se gerere & affectum esse erga ipsos, ut si pereant id fiat propria ipsorum culpa, non quod necessariis auxiliis careant. Quoniam si recte utantur facultatibus & viribus in natura corrupta relictis, Deus paratus est iis prospicere de mediis quibus ad pleniorem cognitionem, adeoque tandem ad veram & salutarem fidem deduci possint.
english: Thesis XIII. God's word is the instrument he ordinarily uses in converting people, yet Calixtus does not hold that those to whom the word has not been preached are left without any means of salvation. God, he says, so acts toward them and is so disposed that if they are lost it is their own fault, not for want of the aids they needed.

If they make right use of the faculties and powers that remain in fallen nature, God stands ready to supply means by which they can be brought to fuller knowledge and so, in the end, to true and saving faith.

source_text: XIV. Postquam enim hanc sibi quaestionem proposuit, Quomodo ad fidem pervenient, qui neque inter Christianos degunt, neque fando unquam quicquam acceperunt de Christianis; a quibus, scilicet, solis verbum audire datur: annon illi sine ulla suae negligentiae culpa pereunt, ideo quod iis Deus non prospexerit, quo verbum sicut aliae gentes audire possent? Inter alia Respondet, Omnibus hominibus superesse aliquas intellectus & voluntatis vires, & naturales notitias, quibus si qui recte usi fuerint, salutis suae curam habuerint, & de ea quantum possunt laboraverint, iis Deum de mediis prospecturum, quibus ad pleniorem & perfectiorem, adeoque revelationi divinae innixam cognitionem deducantur. Cujus rei exemplum nos habere existimat in Cornelio Centurione, & in Eunucho reginae Candaces.
english: Thesis XIV. He puts this question to himself: 'How will people come to faith who neither live among Christians nor have ever heard a word about Christians, from whom alone one can hear the word? Are they not lost without any carelessness on their part, simply because God did not provide for them to hear the word as other nations do?'

Among other things he replies that 'all people keep some powers of intellect and will and some natural knowledge. If any have used these rightly, cared for their salvation, and worked at it as far as they can, God will provide them with means to bring them to a fuller and more complete knowledge, one that rests on divine revelation.' He finds an example of this in Cornelius the centurion and in the eunuch of Queen Candace.

source_text: XV. Quod si autem, inquit, alii horum dissimiles, quae praesto sunt media & auxilia neglexerint, igniculos innatos restinxerint, & veritatem, ut ait Paulus, in injustitia detinuerint, non certe aliquo fato, aut divino decreto, sed propria sua culpa ab illustriore lumine prohibentur. In jam citata Epitome Theologiae pag. 244.
english: Thesis XV. 'But if others, unlike these,' he continues, 'have neglected the means and aids within their reach, put out the sparks born in them, and, as Paul says, held down the truth in unrighteousness, then it is no fate or divine decree but their own fault that shuts them out from the clearer light.'
This is in the Epitome of Theology already cited, page 244.

source_text: XVI. Porro ex antedictis manifestum est, Augustanae Confessionis Theologos non admittere quidem distinctionem gratiae in sufficientem atque efficacem, quae in Schola Romana plurimum usitata est, sed tamen illud ponere quod per gratiam sufficientem plerique Scholae illius Doctores significatum volunt. Nempe illis qui per praedicationem Evangelii non convertuntur, nullum ex parte Dei deesse auxilium quod ad conversionem ipsorum necessarium sit, & sine quo converti non possint: adeoque incredulis ipsis verbum Dei rejicientibus eam offerri gratiam quae abunde sufficiat illis ad poenitentiam & fidem adducendis, si ea uti non recusent.
english: Thesis XVI. It is clear, then, from what has been said, that the theologians of the Augsburg Confession reject the division of grace into sufficient and efficacious, so common in the Roman school, yet affirm what most doctors of that school mean by sufficient grace.

That is: those who are not converted by the preaching of the Gospel lack no aid from God's side that their conversion requires and without which they could not be converted. And so even unbelievers who reject God's word are offered a grace fully enough to bring them to repentance and faith, if they do not refuse to use it.

source_text: XVII. Nec minus evidens est Doctores illos, secundum principia a se posita, non multum laborare ut efficaciam gratiae cum arbitrii humani libertate concilient: quandoquidem statuunt voluntatem ad bonum per gratiam Physice non praedeterminari; nec ullam voluntati per gratiam bene agendi necessitatem imponi: sed hominem libere posse vel gratiae divinae efficaciam admittere, ea per naturam praestando, quae sapientia divina ab eo praeexigit, ut gratia suam in illo efficaciam exerat; vel obicem & impedimentum eidem gratiae ponere, ea negligendo sine quibus gratia in hominem agere non solet, nempe Dei verbum audire, scrutari, atque meditari.
english: Thesis XVII. It is just as plain that, given their own principles, these doctors have little trouble reconciling the efficacy of grace with the freedom of human choice. They hold that grace does not physically predetermine the will to good and lays no necessity of acting well upon it.

A person, rather, is free either to let divine grace be efficacious, by doing through nature what divine wisdom requires of him beforehand so that grace may exercise its efficacy in him, or to set a barrier and hindrance in the way of that grace, by neglecting what grace does not usually act without, namely hearing God's word, studying it, and reflecting on it.

source_text: XVIII. Quae est doctrina Georgii Calixti in citato judicio de Controversiis quae inter Lutheranos & Reformatos agitantur numero 32. Ubi postquam constituit Evangelium esse organum divinum ad fidem & salutem hominibus impertiendum destinatum, cum quo per aures ad mentem immisso conjuncta est gratia divina supernaturalis, per quam praestatur, ut homo qui sibi relictus pridem non poterat assensum & fidem praebere jam possit, subjungit, Facultatem itaque credendi, qua destitutus ante erat, consequitur, necessitate tamen nulla astringitur, quia si indoli & pravitati suae fraenos laxat, potest obsistere & obniti Spiritui Sancto, & Verbum Dei repellere ..... Quod itaque homo Evangelium audiens & considerans credat, imo credere possit, acceptum ferendum est, non naturae viribus, sed gratiae cum Evangelio connexae, & per illud suppeditatae: quod autem gratiae possit refragari, congenitae pravitati & indoli imputandum. Quia enim per gratiam quidem suam Deus efficax est & operatur, non tamen potentia absoluta, sed conditiones & ordinem admittente, inde fit quod successu & eventu frustrari possit.
english: Thesis XVIII. This is Georg Calixtus's doctrine in the judgment already cited on the controversies in dispute between the Lutherans and the Reformed, number 32. There he first establishes that the Gospel is God's appointed instrument for imparting faith and salvation to people. With it, as it enters the mind through the ears, supernatural divine grace is joined, and through that grace a person who, left to himself, could not before give assent and faith is now able to.

Then he adds: 'He thus gains the power of believing that he lacked before, yet no necessity binds him, for if he gives free rein to his disposition and depravity, he can resist and struggle against the Holy Spirit and drive away the word of God ...

That a person who hears and weighs the Gospel believes, or even can believe, must be credited not to the powers of nature but to the grace bound up with the Gospel and supplied through it. That he can withstand grace must be blamed on his inborn depravity and disposition. Since God is indeed efficacious and at work through his grace, though not by absolute power but by a power that allows for conditions and order, it follows that he can be thwarted in the result and outcome.'

source_text: XIX. Neque his repugnat quod dicunt iidem Theologi, conversionem hominis esse unius & solius Spiritus Sancti opus, & hominis voluntatem in conversione pure passive se habere. Nec enim per id negare intendunt actus fidei, spei, timoris, & amoris, in quibus vera ad Deum conversio consistit, esse actus vitales ab hominis voluntate libere elicitos, sed hoc, ad actus istos eliciendos; aliosque similes nihil prorsus valere naturales voluntatis vires; nec voluntatem ulla tenus ex naturalibus illis suis viribus gratiae divinae quae hominem convertit cooperari posse, neque illam quicquam ex suo tribuere, quum Spiritus Sanctus per verbum auditum illam immutare atque innovare aggreditur, & novas vires illi sufficere.
english: Thesis XIX. None of this conflicts with what the same theologians say: that a person's conversion is the work of the Holy Spirit alone, and that in conversion the human will is purely passive.

They do not mean by this to deny that the acts of faith, hope, fear and love that make up true conversion to God are living acts freely produced by a person's will. They mean that the will's natural powers count for nothing at all toward producing those acts, and others like them. Nor can the will, from those natural powers of its own, cooperate in any way with the divine grace that converts a person, or add anything of its own to it, when the Holy Spirit, through the word heard, sets about changing and renewing the will and supplying it with new strength.

source_text: XX. Huc redit quod habet liber Concordiae in Epitome articulorum de quibus controversiae ortae sunt inter Theologos Augustanae confessionis capite de libero arbitrio sub finem. Quod, inquit, Lutherus scripsit, hominis voluntatem in conversione pure passive se habere: id recte & dextre est accipiendum, videlicet, respectu divinae gratiae in accendendis novis motibus. Hoc est, de eo intelligi oportet, quando spiritus Dei per verbum auditum, aut per usum sacramentorum hominis voluntatem aggreditur, & conversionem ac regenerationem in homine operatur. Postquam enim Spiritus Sanctus hoc ipsum jam operatus est, atque effecit, hominisque voluntatem sola sua divina virtute & operatione immutavit atque renovavit: tunc revera hominis nova illa voluntas instrumentum est & organum Spiritus Sancti, ut ea non modo gratiam apprehendat, verum etiam in operibus sequentibus Spiritui Sancto cooperetur. Relinquuntur igitur ante conversionem hominis duae tantum efficientes causae ad conversionem efficaces, nimirum Spiritus Sanctus & verbum Dei, quod est instrumentum Spiritus Sancti, quo conversionem hominis efficit. Hoc verbum homo certe audire debet: sed tamen ut illud ipsum vera fide amplectatur, id nequaquam suis viribus propriis, sed sola gratia & operatione Spiritus Sancti obtinere potest.
english: Thesis XX. The Book of Concord comes to the same thing in the Epitome of the articles in controversy among the theologians of the Augsburg Confession, toward the end of the chapter on free choice. 'Luther's statement,' it says, 'that in conversion the human will is purely passive must be taken rightly and properly, that is, with respect to divine grace in kindling new impulses. It refers to the moment when the Spirit of God, through the word heard or through the use of the sacraments, lays hold of a person's will and works conversion and new birth in him.

Once the Holy Spirit has worked and accomplished this, and by his divine power and working alone has changed and renewed the person's will, then that new will really is the Holy Spirit's instrument and organ: it not only lays hold of grace but also works together with the Holy Spirit in the deeds that follow.

Before a person's conversion, then, only two efficient causes remain that are effective for conversion: the Holy Spirit, and God's word, the Holy Spirit's instrument by which he brings about conversion. A person must certainly hear this word, but he cannot by any strength of his own manage to embrace it with true faith; that comes only by the grace and working of the Holy Spirit.'
